client: I've been feeling really overwhelmed lately since I got promoted at work a few months ago. therapist: Thank you for taking that step and sharing something so personal — what you're describing, that sense of waiting to be "found out," is something a lot of people experience after a big change like a promotion, and it has a name: impostor syndrome. It makes sense that your mind is working overtime right now, and I can hear that this has been weighing on you more than your words might fully capture. I'm glad you're here, and I'd love to start by exploring together what those moments of self-doubt actually look like for you — what kinds of decisions tend to trigger that second-guessing most?

therapist: What you just described is such a common but painful belief — that self-criticism is the engine of your success, and without it everything falls apart. The truth is, research actually shows the opposite: self-compassion tends to make people *more* motivated and resilient, not less, because you're no longer spending so much energy just surviving your own inner voice. I'm curious — can you think of a time when kindness or encouragement, rather than harshness, actually helped you do something well?

therapist: What you just shared takes real courage to look at — that as a child you learned that ordinary wasn't enough, and so you built this inner critic to keep yourself "safe" and striving. I notice you're speaking quite softly right now, like this memory carries a quiet kind of weight rather than just an intellectual understanding, and I want to gently acknowledge that. That little kid who had to work so hard just to feel worthy deserves so much compassion — and I wonder, is it possible that the harsh voice you carry isn't actually *you*, but something you had to borrow just to survive back then?
